mainEntity.name: Is it normal for floss to catch on new composite bonding?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, it's common for floss to catch around new composite bonding as the material creates slightly different surface characteristics compared to natural teeth. Most patients notice some adjustment period as they adapt to the modified tooth contours. However, persistent or worsening catching may indicate areas requiring professional smoothing.

mainEntity.name: Can catching floss damage my composite bonding?

acceptedAnswer.text: Aggressive flossing that repeatedly snags on bonding can potentially cause damage over time, particularly if the floss pulls at loose edges or rough areas. Using gentle techniques and appropriate floss types helps minimise this risk while maintaining effective oral hygiene around bonded teeth.

mainEntity.name: Should I avoid flossing around composite bonding?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, flossing remains essential for maintaining oral health around composite bonding. Avoiding flossing can lead to plaque accumulation and gum disease that may compromise the bonding's longevity. Instead, adapt your technique to work gently around the bonded areas while maintaining thorough cleaning.

mainEntity.name: How often should composite bonding be checked by a dentist?

acceptedAnswer.text: Composite bonding should be evaluated during regular dental check-ups, typically every six months. This allows dentists to assess the bonding's condition, smooth any rough areas that may have developed, and address minor issues before they become problematic for daily oral hygiene.

mainEntity.name: What type of floss works best with composite bonding?

acceptedAnswer.text: Waxed dental floss typically performs better around composite bonding as the wax coating helps it glide more smoothly over slightly irregular surfaces. Some patients also find success with tape-style floss or alternative cleaning tools like water flossers when traditional floss consistently catches.

mainEntity.name: When should I be concerned about floss catching on bonding?

acceptedAnswer.text: Seek professional assessment if floss catching becomes progressively worse, occurs suddenly after a period of normal flossing, or is accompanied by pain, sensitivity, or visible changes in the bonding. Consistent floss shredding or breaking in the same location also warrants evaluation to identify and smooth rough areas.
